Apply \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\), i.e. interchange the two rows of \(A\).

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

Hence the required matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_1 \to R_1 - R_2\). The new first row is

\((1-2,\ -1-5,\ 3-4) = (-1,\ -6,\ -1)\), while \(R_2\) is unchanged.

\(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -6 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

Hence the required matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -6 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(A\), apply \(C_1 \leftrightarrow C_2\) (interchange the columns):

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(B\), apply \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\) (interchange the rows):

\(B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Observation: both transformed matrices are equal, \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 5 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The two given matrices differ only by an interchange, so a column interchange on the first produces the same result as a row interchange on the second.

For \(A\), apply \(2C_2\) (multiply column 2 by 2): \((2\cdot 2,\ 2\cdot 1) = (4,\ 2)\).

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

For \(B\), apply \(-3R_1\) (multiply row 1 by \(-3\)): \((-3\cdot 1,\ -3\cdot 0,\ -3\cdot 2) = (-3,\ 0,\ -6)\).

\(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

Adding the two new matrices:

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & -6 \\ 2 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & -7 \\ 2 & 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\).

Start with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(3R_3\) (multiply row 3 by 3): \((3\cdot 3,\ 3\cdot 3,\ 3\cdot 1) = (9,\ 9,\ 3)\).

\(A \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 9 & 9 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\).

Now apply \(C_3 \to C_3 + 2C_2\): new column 3 is

\((3 + 2(-1),\ 0 + 2(1),\ 3 + 2(9)) = (1,\ 2,\ 21)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 9 & 9 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\).

Hence the required matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 9 & 9 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\).

Start with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(C_3 \to C_3 + 2C_2\) first: new column 3 is

\((3 + 2(-1),\ 0 + 2(1),\ 1 + 2(3)) = (1,\ 2,\ 7)\).

\(A \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 3 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\).

Now apply \(3R_3\) (multiply row 3 by 3): \((3\cdot 3,\ 3\cdot 3,\ 3\cdot 7) = (9,\ 9,\ 21)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 9 & 9 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\).

Conclusion: the final matrix is the same as in Ex. 5, \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 9 & 9 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\). Thus a row transformation and a column transformation can be applied in either order — they are independent, and the result does not depend on the order in which they are performed.

An upper triangular matrix must have zero below the leading diagonal. Here we clear the \((2,1)\) entry.

Apply \(R_2 \to R_2 - 3R_1\): new row 2 is \((3 - 3\cdot 1,\ 4 - 3\cdot 2) = (0,\ -2)\).

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\).

The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\) is upper triangular.

We reduce \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) to the identity by row transformations.

Apply \(R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1\): row 2 becomes \((2 - 2,\ 3 - 2(-1)) = (0,\ 5)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_2 \to \tfrac{1}{5}R_2\): row 2 becomes \((0,\ 1)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

Apply \(R_1 \to R_1 + R_2\): row 1 becomes \((1,\ -1+1) = (1,\ 0)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I\).

Hence the matrix is reduced to the identity matrix \(I\).

We must make the entries below the diagonal — positions \((2,1),(3,1),(3,2)\) — zero using only column transformations. Start with

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

First clear row 3 using \(C_3\) (whose diagonal entry is \(4\)).

Apply \(C_1 \to 4C_1 - 3C_3\): \((4\cdot1-3\cdot2,\ 4\cdot2-3\cdot3,\ 4\cdot3-3\cdot4) = (-2,\ -1,\ 0)\).

Apply \(C_2 \to 4C_2 - 2C_3\): \((4(-1)-2\cdot2,\ 4\cdot1-2\cdot3,\ 4\cdot2-2\cdot4) = (-8,\ -2,\ 0)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} -2 & -8 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

Now clear the \((2,1)\) entry using \(C_2\) (diagonal entry \(-2\)).

Apply \(C_1 \to 2C_1 - C_2\): \((2(-2)-(-8),\ 2(-1)-(-2),\ 0-0) = (4,\ 0,\ 0)\).

\(\sim \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -8 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\).

All entries below the leading diagonal are zero, so this is an upper triangular matrix obtained by column transformations.
